prompt.text: Standard tuning is all fourths except
, which is a major third. Which of these follow from that? Select every one that applies.

spans.text: Strings 3-4-5 and strings 4-5-6 hold identical shapes, because neither uses a string above the break.
A note on a string above the break has to be fretted one fret higher than an all-fourths guitar would need.
Strings 1-2-3 have two notes lifted a fret, and strings 2-3-4 have one.
String 1 is lifted two frets, because it sits two strings above the break.
There are four different geometries to learn, one for each string set.

explanation.text: There is only one irregular jump on the whole neck, so nothing is ever lifted by more than a single fret — string 1 inherits exactly the same shortfall string 2 does. Count the strings a set uses above the break and you have the number of its notes that get lifted: none on strings 3-4-5 and 4-5-6, one on strings 2-3-4, two on strings 1-2-3. That leaves
geometries across the four sets, not four.

prompt.text: You're comping behind a singer, with a bass player and a drummer. Which string set is the safest first choice, and why?

spans.text: Strings 4-5-6 — the lowest set gives the fullest, most supportive sound under a voice.
Strings 1-2-3 — they sit at the top of or above most sung melodies and well clear of the bass, so nothing fights for the same space.
Whichever one your hand is nearest — the set is a reach decision, and the inversion is the musical one.
Strings 3-4-5 — it's the fullest-sounding set, so it works in any arrangement.

explanation.text: The set decides how the chord sits in the music; the inversion decides how far your hand travels — in that order — reaching for whichever set is nearest and calling the inversion the musical choice has it backwards. Strings 4-5-6 is the set most likely to collide with a bass player. Strings 3-4-5 is genuinely the fullest, and that is exactly why it is the first thing you give up when a piano or a second guitar is already there.
